title: Junayd of Baghdad
hook: Junayd of Baghdad, the sober master, who taught the path must hold to the Qur'an and sunnah

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabi'a of Basra, with a torch for paradise and water for hell, in the story people tell of mahabbah. Your line: love for its own sake. Today, a master who loved just as hard and kept his feet on the ground.

Everyone knows someone who falls in love hard. They stop sleeping, write poems at two in the morning, say things they'd never say sober. And everyone knows someone who loves just as deeply and still shows up to work on time, pays the rent and remembers your birthday. Both are real love. Early Sufis had the same two temperaments. Some were famous for their ecstasy, for wild sayings in moments of overwhelming nearness to God. And in Baghdad, around the year 900, there was a master known for the other kind. Later Sufis called him sayyid al-ta'ifa, the master of the whole group.
screen: `TWO KINDS OF LOVE.` → `ECSTASY, OR STEADINESS.` → `BAGHDAD, AROUND 900.`

segments.voice: His name was Abu al-Qasim al-Junayd, and he died in Baghdad around the year 910. He learned the path from his uncle, a Sufi teacher named Sari al-Saqati, and he studied the law, deeply. Later writers used two words for the two temperaments on the path. Sukr: intoxication, being overwhelmed, carried away. And sahw: sobriety, coming back to yourself. Junayd is remembered as the great master of sobriety. For him, the highest point wasn't getting lost in ecstasy and staying there. It was being drawn close to God, then coming back, awake, to an ordinary life of prayer, work and kindness, with that nearness still inside. His best-known rule, as the early Sufi handbooks report it, goes roughly like this: our knowledge is tied to the Qur'an and the sunnah, and whoever hasn't learned the Qur'an and written down hadith shouldn't be followed in this path. No inner experience gets to overrule the Book. That made him a bridge. Scholars of the law who distrusted Sufis could respect Junayd, and many later Sufi chains of teachers pass through his name. Some of the ecstatic Sufis said things that shocked their neighbors, and there were real conflicts over it. Junayd's way was careful: love God with everything, and keep your feet on the ground of the law. Sober love.
screen: `SARI'S NEPHEW, AND A SCHOLAR OF LAW.` · `SUKR AND SAHW — DRUNK AND SOBER.` · `TIED TO THE QUR'AN AND SUNNAH.` · `A BRIDGE BETWEEN LAW AND LOVE.` · then, large: `SOBER LOVE.`

segments.voice: Choose one small, steady rule to keep, nothing glamorous: no phone at the table, on time for one thing, a promise kept. Then choose one moment of prayer or stillness to keep too: a prayer at its time, if you pray, or a quiet minute, if you don't. One for the feet, one for the heart; hold both in mind now.
Sahw. Sobriety, coming back to yourself after being drawn near to God — the mark of Junayd of Baghdad's path. Today's word.
Your line: sober love. Drawn near, then back to prayer, work and kindness. Day two hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Many Sufi orders trace their teaching through Junayd and follow his insistence that the inner path stay within the Qur'an, the sunnah and the law; his letters and sayings are studied in Sufi handbooks.
